title: Understanding GitHub Pages, URLs, and Version History
body: During the deployment process, the system verifies that the URLs for the local server and GitHub Pages, as well as the app version string, match.
detail: For static web apps deployed via GitHub Pages, the files visible locally may differ from those visible at the actual public URL. Therefore, you should first verify them on the local_server, and after pushing, verify again that the `index.html`, `app.js`, and JSON files at the GitHub Pages URL are up to date. Version strings, such as `app_data_version`, serve as a reference for determining whether the cache is displaying outdated files.
examples: On your local machine, first check the URL http://127.0.0.1:5173/.
After deployment, check the `APP_DATA_VERSION` in `app.js` on GitHub Pages.

title: Reading the Evidence·Lineage·Provenance Flow
body: Evidence supports a decision; provenance and lineage trace a source through transformations. Filenames and line numbers are convenient but can drift after edits, so also record stable source IDs, a version or hash, extraction time, and transformations. Verify that each citation actually supports its claim.
examples: Include the source filename and line number next to your answer.
Record the steps taken from the raw data to the processed results.

title: Understanding the Batch·Shard·Memory Flow
body: Divide large tasks into batches and shards, and process them while monitoring memory usage.
detail: A "batch" is a unit that groups multiple items for processing, while a "shard" is a large dataset divided into multiple pieces. Reading a `large_file` all at once can cause memory issues, so it needs to be processed line by line or in small batches. Concurrency is a method of executing multiple tasks simultaneously, but increasing it too much can lead to failures and memory shortages before any speed gains are realized.
examples: Large JSONL files are processed by reading them one line at a time.
The files are split into parts such as shard_001 and shard_002 for parallel processing.

title: Understanding the Environment·main·checklist Workflow
body: The execution environment, the `main` entry point, and the checklist are the basic steps for running the script reliably.
detail: The environment refers to the conditions under which the code runs. The same code may behave differently depending on the Python version, installed packages, current directory, and environment variables. `main` is the point where the script actually begins, and the checklist summarizes the conditions that should be verified before and after execution. If a `parse_error` occurs, you should first determine whether the issue is due to a syntax error or a problem with the input file format.
examples: The execution flow begins below if __name__ == '__main__':.
Before execution, it checks whether the current folder and the input file exist.

title: Understanding the Count·Filter·Aggregation Flow
body: Many data summarization processes involve filtering the data, counting the number of records, and aggregating the results by group.
detail: Filtering is the process of retaining only the necessary items, while counting is the process of determining the number of items that meet a given condition. Aggregation involves grouping multiple values to produce summary statistics such as totals, averages, and distributions. If there are classification values such as “level,” you can calculate the count or percentage for each level. When reading code, you should check the order to determine whether the filter conditions come first or the aggregation comes first.
examples: Count the number of cards that are at the beginner level.
Use a counter to count the number of cards per file.

title: Understanding Rollback, Separation, and UI Flow
body: Keep UI changes and logic changes separate, and manage them so that they can be rolled back if a problem arises.
detail: Separation is a design approach that divides roles. For example, CSS is responsible for the visual appearance of the screen, while JavaScript logic handles data processing and user interaction. UI changes have a significant visual impact, but when they are mixed with logic errors, it becomes difficult to pinpoint the source of the problem. Rollback is the process of reverting a problematic change to its previous state. Breaking commits into smaller units makes rollbacks easier.
examples: Whenever possible, separate CSS changes and JSON data changes into separate commits.
If a problem arises, check the most recent commit to narrow down the scope of the changes.
